description: African Library and Information Associations & Institutions (AfLIA) is the trusted African voice for the library and information community, and drives equitable access to information and knowledge for all. AfLIA is an independent international not-for-profit organization which pursues the interests of library and information associations, library and information services, librarians and information workers and the communities they serve in Africa

AIF works at improving the quality of education and learning skills in madrasas and school going pre-primary and primary children with learning and remedial centers in more than 70 villages in three blocks of Pothia, Kishanganj and Thakurganj. Currently more than 3500 children, half of them girls are studying in the learning centers.

CGNet Swara is working with the Gond tribe to safeguard the language for the coming generations by helping build a repository of Gondi books for the coming generation of tribal children and also, use these data sets as input for building a Gondi machine translation tool.

North East Educational Trust runs a library programme to enhance children’s ability of critical thinking and creative expression. Currently, we support 4 government schools in conducting regular library sessions in Kamrup(metro) district of Assam and operate NEET’s Community library located in Guwahati.  Around 500 students have benefitted from our library programme in schools and 150 from NEET’s Community Library.

The Uganda Christian University’s (UCU) aims to supplement early literacy initiatives by making quality multilingual children stories freely available to the local communities. This is a part of the UCU Community Service Project: ‘Creative Writing, Translation and Publishing for Children’ in the Department of Languages and Literature. The project also seeks to print these stories and make them accessible to all children of the local communities in Uganda through the UCU campuses and colleges.

description: Working in 25 villages in Birbhum, West Bengal, and reaching about 1500 adivasi children, Suchana contributes to making learning more relevant, accessible, and successful for this group through supplementary learning interventions. These include integrating technology in learning and a strong focus on first language learning, especially in early years.

Pratham Books is a not-for-profit children’s book publisher with a mission to ‘put a book in every child’s hand’.’ The key objective is to publish good quality, affordable storybooks in multiple Indian languages to support reading acquisition among children. In the last decade, Pratham Books has published over 350+ original titles in 21 Indian languages, which total up to about 2500+ books. The books cover a range of genres including early readers, fiction, non-fiction, and storybooks on science, history, mathematics and nature.  Pratham Books had the distinction of working with many of the country's renowned authors and illustrators and their books have won several awards as well.

Darakht-e Danesh Library, a digital repository of open educational resources (OERs) in Afghanistan, creates access to quality, locally adapted educational resources and supports teachers to use, adapt, create and share their own resources. The DD Library currently houses more than 3,000 resources in Dari, Pashto, English, and minority languages like Nooristani, Uzbeki and Hazaragi.

Chippersage is committed to delivering learning solutions and tools that enhance English language skills for all learners irrespective of age and proficiency levels. They've designed modules to ensure Listening, Reading, Speaking and Writing skills, all the aspects required for language fluency, are nurtured and strengthened.

In its most common sense as "a colorful conspicuous structure", the word flower includes many structures which are not anatomically flowers in the botanical sense. Sunflowers and daisies, for example, are structurally clusters of many small flowers that together appear to be a single flower (a capitulum, a form of pseudanthium), but these are considered to be flowers in the general sense.
